channel.title: Tools on Open History Map
channel.description: Recent content in Tools on Open History Map

item.title: GeoContext Editor
item.description:
A standalone desktop application — built with Tauri v2 and SvelteKit — for working on Geocontext repositories directly, following the same FORMAT.md as the Geocontext Front-End.

Where the QGIS plugin captures a bundle from an existing GIS project and the web front-end renders one for readers, the editor sits in between: open a gcx.json, edit its manifest and datasets, and commit the result — no QGIS session required.

Part of the GeoContext project.

item.title: Harris MCP
item.description:
The Harris matrix is how archaeologists record stratigraphy: the ordered relationships between the layers and cuts of an excavation. harris-mcp exposes those matrices to LLM agents through the Model Context Protocol, with adapters for the common interchange formats — HMDP, CSV, XLSX and HMC/HMCX.

The read surface is tuned for language models; the write surface is changelog-backed, so every edit an agent makes is auditable and reversible. Corpus-level tools let it reason across a whole set of documents at once.

item.title: Index API
item.description:
OHM’s sources live in Zotero, tagged with ohm:* descriptors by the Zotero plugin. This API is what turns that library into a public, queryable index: it connects to Zotero, reads the curated items and their descriptors, and serves them as the searchable catalogue behind index.openhistorymap.org.

Pair it with the Index Front-End for the browser side of the same service.

item.title: Index Front-End
item.description:
The reading side of the data index: a browser interface for searching the sources, datasets and ohm:* descriptors that the Index API serves.

It is where a researcher goes to ask what does OHM know about this place, this period, this theme — and to trace any answer back to the Zotero item it came from.

item.title: Archaeo Pro
item.description:
A tool for the paperwork that surrounds Italian sorveglianze archeologiche — the archaeological surveillance carried out alongside construction work. It is a field-first progressive web app: record observations on site, including offline, then turn them into the required DOCX/PDF reports.

The same records can be exported to Open History Map, so surveillance fieldwork feeds the wider dataset rather than ending in a filing cabinet. A FastAPI + PostGIS back-end handles storage and the spatial side.

item.title: Tiles API (Rust)
item.description:
A reimplementation of the Tiles API in Rust: same time-, space- and layer-aware vector tiles, served read-only through axum over a deadpool-postgres connection pool, emitting standard MVT.

The goal is the same contract as the Python server at a lower resource cost — a drop-in tile back-end for high-traffic or constrained deployments. It is the newer of the two and still being hardened against the original.

item.title: Tiles Archive
item.description:
The live Tiles API generates tiles on demand; this tool bakes them. It slices the data by time partition, writes each slice out as a single-file PMTiles archive, and publishes the result to Cloudflare R2.

The payoff is static hosting: a PMTiles file on object storage serves a whole time window straight to the client, no tile server in the loop — cheaper to run and trivial to cache or mirror.

item.title: HGTFS — Historical General Transit Feed Specification
item.description:
GTFS describes today’s transit networks; HGTFS is the equivalent for historical ones. Every stop, route, network edge and operator carries an explicit time-of-validity, so a network can be reconstructed for any chosen date — and where the historical record is uncertain, the dates say so (date_opened bounded by min/max, closures asserted only on evidence).

The specification is developed in the open at hgtfs.github.io — a full field reference plus a time-aware web viewer that scrubs a feed through time and recolours the network as operators change. It grew out of the earlier, archived openhistorymap/HTFS draft and is the basis for transit layers inside OHM.

item.title: Map Styles
item.description: A small repository of MapLibre / Mapbox-style JSON definitions used to render the OHM tile layers. Useful if you want to embed an OHM map in your own site, or fork a style as a starting point for a custom historical cartography.

item.title: OHM Map
item.description:
The OHM web client is the canonical entry point to the project’s data: a MapLibre-based interface that lets you pan and zoom across geography and across time, switching between historical layers, base maps and thematic overlays.

It is the public face of the platform; the rest of the stack on this page exists either to feed it data, or to extend the workflow around it.

item.title: OHM Zotero Plugin
item.description:
The OHM data pipeline is rooted in Zotero: each source — a paper, a map, a chronicle, a dataset — lives as a Zotero item, and OHM-specific metadata is carried as ohm:* tags on that item.

This plugin adds dedicated UI for editing those descriptors, so curators can work directly in Zotero rather than maintaining a parallel spreadsheet. Pair it with the Chrome extension below to capture sources from the web.

item.title: Tiles API
item.description:
The tiles API is the server that backs the map. Standard XYZ tile servers key tiles by (z, x, y); OHM data also has a temporal axis, so the API adds time-window filtering and per-layer grouping on top of the usual spatial pyramid.

It is the longest-running piece of OHM-specific infrastructure and underpins every map view we publish.

item.title: OHM Zotero Chrome Extension
item.description:
A small Chrome extension that lives next to the Zotero Connector and fills a specific gap: attaching arbitrary web pages as linked URL attachments to an item that already exists in your library.

Used together with the OHM Zotero plugin, it turns the everyday research browser into a one-click pipeline for enriching OHM source records.

item.title: Geocontext Front-End
item.description:
The companion to the QGIS plugin: a static front-end that reads a gcx.json manifest and renders the referenced GeoJSON datasets on an interactive map.

It is designed to be hosted alongside the bundle itself — drop the front-end and a Geocontext repository on the same host (or on GitHub Pages) and the bundle becomes a self-contained, shareable atlas.

Part of the GeoContext project.

item.title: Geocontext QGIS Plugin
item.description:
A QGIS plugin aimed at researchers who already work in QGIS and want to publish a slice of their project as an open, shareable bundle.

The plugin captures the current view — extents, layers and selected datasets — and writes them out as a gcx.json manifest plus datasets/*.geojson, then optionally pushes the result to a GitHub repository via the system git. The matching front-end (see Geocontext Front-End) renders these bundles back to a browser.

item.title: Historical Street View API
item.description:
Photography only goes back to the late 18th century, but humans have been making located views of the world for far longer. The Historical Street View project collects those views and lets you walk through them on a map, choosing both where and when you stand.

hsv-api is the back-end that serves those located views; visions.ofthepast.org is the public front-end built on top of it.
